newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing CEO confident of approval of MCDonnell deal.
newsitem.headline: Boeing CEO confident of approval of MCDonnell deal.

text.p: Boeing Co appeared confident on Tuesday that it would get clearance in both the European Union and the United States for its merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp .

Boeing chairman and chief executive officer Phil Condit told a lunch gathering before meeting European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert that the deal would have little effect on Boeing's position in the civil aviation market.
Whether or not Boeing merged with its Saint Louis-based defence and aviation competitor, the market was already dominated by Boeing and the European Airbus Industry consortium.

"In terms of changes in market share this (deal) does almost nothing. Best estimates, I think by both Airbus and ourselves, are that neither of our market share changes all that much," Condit told the European Aviation Club.

Contrasting with Condit's optimism, Van Miert has said several times that the deal was complicated and that the Commission would need time to assess carefully its impact on fair competition in the 15-nation bloc.
The Commission is expected to start an in-depth probe into the alliance by March 19, when it concludes its preliminary one-month investigation.
Boeing has said it is expecting to clear all regulatory hurdles on both sides of the Atlantic by July. The alliance announced in December was also filed with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.
Condit stressed that with a three-percent share of the commercial aviation market McDonnell Douglas "was not a significant player".
He drew a parallel between Boeing's latest alliance and its acquisition in 1996 of the defence and aerospace units of Rockwell Intenational Corp.
As in the Rockwell case, there was almost no overlap between the activities of the Seattle-based aircraft giant and and McDonnell's.

Boeing has about 60 percent of the world's civil aviation market against 35 percent for Airbus. Airbus partners are France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace , Spain's CASA and Daimler-Benz of Germany.

Condit said the alliance with McDonnell had been determined by the need to better balance Boeing's businesses from its heavy dependence on commercial aircraft, which currently represent 80 percent of its revenue, to defence and space.
As a result of the deal, the second market would account for 40 percent of Boeing's revenue.
Condit declined to comment on his meeting with Van Miert, saying he would be doing a lot of listening and explaining the "rationale" behing the merger.

Condit also repeated that it was not in Boeing's plans to develop a "superjumbo" jet, because he did not think there was a big market for it. Airbus is planning a 555-seat large aircraft, dubbed A3XX, to rival Boeing's 747 Jumbo jet.
But the project had not been altogether dropped: "If I was approached over the possibility of doing (something) jointly I would look at it", he said in reply to questions.
